title: Choose a conditional that fits the situation

variants.label: と · regular consequence

segments.role: と presents a predictable consequence. It ordinarily does not introduce a personal request or invitation as that consequence.

example.translation: When it rains, the road becomes slippery.

variants.change: と presents a predictable consequence. It ordinarily does not introduce a personal request or invitation as that consequence.

variants.label: ば · condition

segments.role: ば foregrounds the condition under which the result holds. Restrictions on volitional continuations depend on the clause and subject.

example.translation: If it rains, the road becomes slippery.
example.note: Focus on the condition for the result.

variants.change: ば foregrounds the condition under which the result holds. Restrictions on volitional continuations depend on the clause and subject.

variants.label: たら · once / if

segments.role: たら can introduce an instruction for when the condition is met. The full main clause changes to make that use visible.

example.translation: If it rains, please wear shoes that do not slip easily.
example.note: An instruction for after the condition is met.

variants.change: たら can introduce an instruction for when the condition is met. The full main clause changes to make that use visible.

variants.label: なら · given that

segments.role: なら takes the proposed rain as a premise. The preparation can occur before the rain itself.

example.translation: If it is going to rain, let us change shoes first.
example.note: A forecast becomes the premise for preparation.

variants.change: なら takes the proposed rain as a premise. The preparation can occur before the rain itself.

question: Which construction naturally frames a forecast as a premise for doing something beforehand?
answers: 雨が降るなら、先に靴を替えましょう。
雨が降ると、先に靴を替えましょう。
feedback: なら can take a proposed situation as a premise for advice or preparation. Regular-consequence と is unsuitable for this ordinary invitation.
